### 🎯 Practical Learning Objectives (Week 3)

By the end of this practical session, you should be able to:

- **Generate** basic **summary statistics** for numerical and categorical data.
- **Use** `summary()`, `mean()`, `median()`, `sd()`, `count()` and related functions to summarise datasets.
- **Plot and interpret** **bar charts**, **histograms**, **boxplots** and **scatter plots** with `ggplot2`.
- **Comment** on patterns, trends, and possible relationships observed in the plots.

> 💡 This notebook focuses on **hands-on EDA**. You are expected to run, modify, and extend the examples using your own dataset where possible.

## 4. Generating Summary Statistics

We start EDA by computing summary statistics for **numerical** and **categorical** features. Common functions:

- `summary(df)` – summary of every column.
- `mean(df$col)`, `median(df$col)`, `sd(df$col)` – single statistics.
- `count(df, col)` – frequency table for a categorical column.

For a numeric variable $x_1, \dots, x_n$:

$$\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i, \qquad
s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_i - \bar{x}\right)^2}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\bar{x}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.$$

```{r summary-all}
# Summary of every column (numbers: quartiles and mean; factors: counts)
summary(df)
```

```{r summary-one}
# Statistics for ONE numerical column
num_col <- "Age"                  # TODO: change to another numeric column (e.g. "Fare")
x <- df[[num_col]]                # [[ ]] extracts a column by name stored in a variable

cat("n                  :", length(x), "\n")
cat("Mean               :", round(mean(x), 2), "\n")
cat("Median             :", round(median(x), 2), "\n")
cat("Standard deviation :", round(sd(x), 2), "\n")
cat("IQR                :", round(IQR(x), 2), "\n")
cat("Min / Max          :", min(x), "/", max(x), "\n")

# 95% confidence interval for the mean (t-distribution)
ci <- t.test(x)$conf.int
cat("95% CI for the mean: [", round(ci[1], 2), ",", round(ci[2], 2), "]\n")
```

> 💡 **Reading the numbers:** if the **mean is much larger than the median**, the distribution is probably *right-skewed* (a few very large values pull the mean up). The standard deviation tells you the typical distance of a value from the mean.

## 5. Visualising Categorical Data with Bar Charts

Bar charts are useful for showing the frequency of categories (e.g., gender, department, grade). In `ggplot2` every chart is built in layers: **data** → **aesthetics** (`aes`: what maps to x, y, colour) → **geometry** (`geom_*`: bars, points, lines) → **labels and theme**.

```{r bar-chart}
cat_col <- "Embarked"             # TODO: change to another categorical variable

ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[cat_col]])) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(title = paste("Bar chart of", cat_col), x = cat_col, y = "Count")
```

A bar chart can also show a **second variable** through colour. Here the bars are scaled to 100% so that proportions are comparable across groups:

```{r bar-fill}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Pclass, fill = Survived)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(No = "grey65", Yes = "seagreen")) +
  labs(title = "Survival rate by passenger class", x = "Class", y = "Share of passengers", fill = "Survived")
```

## 6. Visualising Numerical Data with Histograms and Boxplots

Histograms help you understand the **distribution** of a numerical variable (scores, ages, income):

- Is the distribution **symmetric** or **skewed**?
- Are there **multiple peaks**?
- Are there **outliers** (very large or small values)?

```{r histogram}
num_col <- "Age"                  # TODO: change to a different numeric variable

ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[num_col]])) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                 fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +     # smooth density curve
  labs(title = paste("Histogram of", num_col), x = num_col, y = "Density")
```

A **boxplot** summarises the distribution with five numbers (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and flags potential outliers (points beyond $1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}$ from the box):

```{r boxplot}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Pclass, y = Fare, fill = Pclass)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Fare by passenger class", x = "Class", y = "Fare (pounds)")
```

## 7. Exploring Relationships with Scatter Plots

Scatter plots help you investigate relationships between **two numerical variables**, for example hours studied vs exam score, age vs income, price vs quantity sold. For two variables the **Pearson correlation coefficient** is

$$r = \frac{\sum_{i}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2}\sqrt{\sum_i (y_i-\bar{y})^2}}, \qquad -1 \le r \le 1.$$

```{r scatter}
x_col <- "Age"       # TODO: change to a real numerical column (x-axis)
y_col <- "Fare"      # TODO: change to a real numerical column (y-axis)

ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[x_col]], y = .data[[y_col]])) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = paste("Scatter plot of", y_col, "vs", x_col), x = x_col, y = y_col)
```

```{r correlation}
# Pearson correlation with 95% confidence interval and p-value
ct <- cor.test(df[[x_col]], df[[y_col]])
cat(sprintf("Pearson r = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f], p = %.4f, n = %d\n",
            ct$estimate, ct$conf.int[1], ct$conf.int[2], ct$p.value, nrow(df)))

# Spearman rank correlation: robust to skewed variables such as Fare
cs <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(df[[x_col]], df[[y_col]], method = "spearman"))
cat(sprintf("Spearman rho = %.3f, p = %.4f\n", cs$estimate, cs$p.value))
```
